arXiv:2601.15990v2 [math.AP] 28 Jan 2026

A SHARP CRITERION AND COMPLETE CLASSIFICATION OF GLOBAL-IN-TIME SOLUTIONS AND FINITE TIME BLOW-UP OF SOLUTIONS TO A CHEMOTAXIS SYSTEM IN SUPERCRITICAL DIMENSIONS

August 24, 2026
Abstract

We consider the chemotaxis system with indirect signal production in the whole space,

{ut=Δu−∇⋅(u∇v),0=Δ​v+w,wt=Δ​w+u\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v),\\ 0=\Delta v+w,\\ w_{t}=\Delta w+u\end{cases} (⋆\star)

with emphasis on supercritical dimensions. In contrast to the classical parabolic-elliptic Keller–Segel system, where the analysis can be reduced to a single equation, the above system is essentially parabolic-parabolic and does not admit such a reduction. In this paper, we establish a sharp threshold phenomenon separating global-in-time existence from finite time blow-up in terms of scaling-critical Morrey norms of the initial data. In particular, we prove the existence of singular stationary solutions and show that their Morrey norm values serve as the critical thresholds determining the long-time behavior of solutions. Consequently, we identify new critical exponents at which the long-time behavior of solutions changes. This yields a complete classification of the long-time behavior of solutions, providing the first such results for the essentially parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis system ( ⋆ ) in supercritical dimensions.

†† 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary 35K55; Secondary 35B44, 35B51, 35Q92†† Key words and phrases. chemotaxis, blowup, global existence, comparison principles

1 Introduction

1.1 Biological and Mathematical Background

Chemotaxis refers to the directed movement of cells in response to gradients of chemical signals and plays a crucial role in a variety of biological phenomena. Examples include aggregation and pattern formation in microbial populations, as well as coordinated cell migration in developmental and pathological processes. These observations have inspired extensive mathematical studies of chemotaxis models, most notably those based on systems of partial differential equations. Among them, the Keller–Segel model (cf. (1.2) below), originally introduced by Keller and Segel [28] to describe the migration of cells guided by chemical signals generated by the cell population itself, has long served as a fundamental model in the study of chemotaxis. Originally motivated by biological observations, the Keller–Segel model has also stimulated extensive mathematical research over the years, leading to a deeper understanding of its structural and dynamical properties (see [5, 12, 13, 22, 23, 37, 35, 36, 3]). In this paper, we consider the Cauchy problem for the chemotaxis system:

{ut=Δu−∇⋅(u∇v)in​ℝd×(0,∞),0=Δ​v+win​ℝd×(0,∞),wt=Δ​w+uin​ℝd×(0,∞),(u⁡(⋅,0),w⁡(⋅,0))=(u0​(⋅),w0​(⋅))in​ℝd.\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)\qquad&\mathrm{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,\infty),\\ 0=\Delta v+w\qquad&\mathrm{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,\infty),\\ w_{t}=\Delta w+u\qquad&\mathrm{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,\infty),\\ (u(\cdot,0),w(\cdot,0))=(u_{0}(\cdot),w_{0}(\cdot))\qquad&\mathrm{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{d}.\end{cases} (P)

The system (P) features an indirect signal production mechanism, where the chemoattractant potential vv is determined elliptically from an intermediate variable ww, while ww itself evolves according to a parabolic equation driven by the cell density uu. The system (P) can be regarded as a simplified version of the chemotaxis model:

{ut=Δu−∇⋅(u∇v)in​Ω×(0,∞),τ1​vt=γ1​Δ​v−δ1​v+win​Ω×(0,∞),τ2​wt=γ2​Δ​w−δ2​w+uin​Ω×(0,∞),\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \tau_{1}v_{t}=\gamma_{1}\Delta v-\delta_{1}v+w&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \tau_{2}w_{t}=\gamma_{2}\Delta w-\delta_{2}w+u&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega\times(0,\infty),\end{cases} (1.1)

where Ω\Omega is either a bounded domain or the whole space and the parameters τ1,τ2,γ1,γ2,δ1,δ2\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\delta_{1},\delta_{2} are nonnegative. The chemotaxis model (1.1) is a specific instance of a system proposed by [31] in the context of biological processes related to Alzheimer’s disease. In particular, the model (1.1) with γ2=0\gamma_{2}=0 has also been used to model the cluster attack behavior of the Mountain Pine Beetle, as proposed in [40]. From a mathematical point of view, the chemotaxis model (1.1) has been studied in various parameter regimes. In the fully parabolic case, several analytical results are available in the literature (see [17, 18, 24, 25], for instance). On the other hand, when γ2=0\gamma_{2}=0 the system reduces to a parabolic–parabolic–ODE (or parabolic–elliptic–ODE) type, for which different aspects of solutions behavior have been investigated in recent years (see [30, 39, 41], for instance).

1.2 Mass critical phenomena in critical dimensions

The system (P) can be viewed as a variant of the classical Keller–Segel system:

{ut=Δu−∇⋅(u∇v),τ​vt=Δ​v+u\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v),\\ \tau v_{t}=\Delta v+u\end{cases} (1.2)

in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, where the parameter τ\tau is nonnegative. The Keller–Segel system enjoys the scaling invariance:

uλ​(x,t)=λ2​u​(λ​x,λ2​t),vλ​(x,t)=v⁡(λ​x,λ2​t)for​λ>0.\displaystyle u_{\lambda}(x,t)=\lambda^{2}u(\lambda x,\lambda^{2}t),\quad v_{\lambda}(x,t)=v(\lambda x,\lambda^{2}t)\quad\mathrm{for}\ \lambda>0. (1.3)

In addition, from a biological modeling perspective, the Keller–Segel system is expected to satisfy the mass conservation law ‖u⁡(t)‖L1​(ℝ2)=‖u0‖L1​(ℝ2)\|u(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}, which follows from the fact that the first equation is written in divergence form. Consequently, the L1L^{1}-norm of uu plays a distinguished role. The scaling leaves the L1L^{1}-norm invariant if and only if the spatial dimension satisfies d=2d=2, which therefore constitutes the critical dimension. In view of the above observations, the two-dimensional case occupies a distinguished position in the theory of the Keller–Segel system, both in bounded domains and in the whole space. Indeed, in two space dimensions, the long-time behavior of solutions of (1.2) is known to depend sensitively on the total initial mass. This criticality gives rise to a threshold phenomenon separating global existence from blow-up, which is commonly referred to as the 8​π8\pi-problem. More precisely, when the initial cell density u0u_{0} with radial symmetry is given by a nonnegative measure whose total mass satisfies ‖u0‖L1<8​π\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}}<8\pi, the corresponding radial solution remains well-defined for all t>0t>0 and does not develop singularities (see [36, 12, 10, 33, 14]). While if ‖u0‖L1>8​π\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}}>8\pi, then a finite time blow-up may occur (see [37, 35, 22, 23, 34, 10]).

The systems (P) and (1.1) with δ1=δ2=0\delta_{1}=\delta_{2}=0 admit a scaling transformation analogous to that of the Keller–Segel system. Nevertheless, due to its indirect signal production mechanism, the associated scaling properties lead to a distinct notion of criticality. Indeed these systems are invariant under the natural scaling: for λ>0\lambda>0

uλ​(x,t)=λ4​u​(λ​x,λ2​t),vλ​(x,t)=v⁡(λ​x,λ2​t),wλ​(x,t)=λ2​w​(λ​x,λ2​t).\displaystyle u_{\lambda}(x,t)=\lambda^{4}u(\lambda x,\lambda^{2}t),\quad v_{\lambda}(x,t)=v(\lambda x,\lambda^{2}t),\quad w_{\lambda}(x,t)=\lambda^{2}w(\lambda x,\lambda^{2}t). (1.4)

Under this scaling, the critical dimension in the above sense is d=4d=4. Indeed, in [17, 18], the authors revealed several characteristic features of solutions to (1.1) in the critical dimension d=4d=4 on bounded domains. Here, we restrict ourselves to the case where all parameters are set equal to one. If one has the assumption that the initial data (u0,v0,w0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}) satisfies ‖u0‖L1​(Ω)<(8​π)2\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}<(8\pi)^{2}, then the corresponding solution of (1.1) exists globally in time and remains uniformly bounded in time, whereas it was shown that there exists the initial data such that ‖u0‖L1​(Ω)∈((8​π)2,∞)∖(8​π)2​ℕ\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}\in((8\pi)^{2},\infty)\setminus(8\pi)^{2}\mathbb{N} and the corresponding solution blows up. In the whole space ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}, it was proved in [24] that the solution to (1.1) exists globally in time whenever ‖u0‖L1​(ℝ4)<(8​π)2\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{4})}<(8\pi)^{2}.

Such mass critical phenomena are characteristic of scale critical dimensions and are absent in higher, supercritical settings. This naturally raises the question of what determines the long-time dynamics of solutions to (P) and (1.1), and (1.2) when the systems are considered in supercritical dimensions.

1.3 Parabolic-elliptic model in higher dimensions d≥3d\geq 3

In this subsection, we consider the Keller–Segel system (1.2) with τ=0\tau=0 corresponding to the parabolic-elliptic case:

{ut=Δu−∇⋅(u∇v)in​ℝd×(0,∞),0=Δ​v+uin​ℝd×(0,∞)\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)\qquad&\mathrm{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,\infty),\\ 0=\Delta v+u\qquad&\mathrm{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\end{cases} (1.5)

and discuss the long-time behavior of its solutions in supercritical dimensions. As noted in previous subsection, a central issue is to identify the mechanisms that control the long-time behavior of solutions. One possible perspective for addressing this issue is provided by the existence of a singular stationary solution, such as the well-known Chandrasekhar steady state solution in [15]

uC​(x)=2​(d−2)|x|2.\displaystyle u_{C}(x)=\dfrac{2(d-2)}{|x|^{2}}.

Indeed, such singular stationary solution plays a crucial role in the analysis in supercritical dimensions of the solutions to the simplified Keller–Segel system (1.5). In this context, two different criteria have been employed to characterize the role of the singular stationary solution uCu_{C} in the dynamics of (1.5).

One approach is based on conditions formulated in terms of critical Morrey norms. For instance, according to [7], if the initial data u0u_{0} with radially symmetry belongs to the critical Morrey space Md2​(ℝd)M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) which are invariant under the scaling argument (1.3), and satisfies the upper bound

‖u0‖Md2​(ℝd)<2​σd=‖uC‖Md2​(ℝd),\displaystyle\|u_{0}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}<2\sigma_{d}=\|u_{C}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})},

where σd\sigma_{d} is the measure of the unit sphere in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, then corresponding solution of (1.5) exists globally in time in an appropriate functional class and enjoys the same bound

‖u⁡(t)‖Md2​(ℝd)​<2​σdfor​all​t>​0.\displaystyle\|u(t)\|_{M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}<2\sigma_{d}\quad\mathrm{for\ all}\ t>0.

Moreover, it was also demonstrated in [38] that for some initial data with ‖u0‖Md2​(ℝd)>2​σd\|u_{0}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}>2\sigma_{d}, the behavior of the corresponding solution to (1.5) depends on the spatial dimension dd. In dimensions d≥10d\geq 10, one can choose such u0u_{0} so that the corresponding solution of (1.5) blows up in finite time, whereas in dimensions 3≤d≤93\leq d\leq 9, there exists initial data with the same condition such that the corresponding solution of (1.5) exists globally in time.

Another approach focuses on a direct comparison between the initial data and the singular stationary solution itself. Recently, [45] established that, whenever the initial data u0∈B​U​C​(ℝd)u_{0}\in BUC(\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfies u0≤uCu_{0}\leq u_{C}, (1.5) admits a unique global classical solution and the solution enjoys the upper bound:

‖u⁡(t)‖Md2​(ℝd)≤2​σdfor​all​t>0.\displaystyle\|u(t)\|_{M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq 2\sigma_{d}\quad\mathrm{for\ all}\ t>0.

Furthermore, it was shown in [45] that, in dimensions d≥10d\geq 10, if initial data satisfies the asymptotic condition:

lim inf|x|→∞|x|2​u0​(x)>2​(d−2),\displaystyle\liminf_{|x|\to\infty}|x|^{2}u_{0}(x)>2(d-2),

which implies that the decay of u0u_{0} at infinity is slower than that of the singular stationary solution uCu_{C}, then the corresponding solution blows up in finite time. Consequently, in supercritical dimensions, the behavior of initial data at spatial infinity is key to the analysis of the long-time dynamics of solutions to (1.5). In particular, the singular stationary solution uCu_{C} appears to act as a critical threshold separating different qualitative behaviors of solutions to (1.5).

1.4 Statement of the problem

The aim of the present paper is to provide a detailed description of the behavior of the solutions to (P) in the supercritical case d≥5d\geq 5. As noted in the previous subsection, extensive studies on supercritical dimensions have been carried out for the simplified Keller–Segel system (1.5). These results crucially rely on the fact that, in the parabolic-elliptic setting, the second equation reduces to a Poisson-type equation. A key feature of the Poisson-type structure is that it effectively reduces the system to a single equation for the cell density through the use of a so-called mass function. In fact, once the mass function is defined in this manner U⁡(r,t)=r−d​∫0rρd−1​u​(ρ,t)​𝑑ρU(r,t)=r^{-d}\int_{0}^{r}\rho^{d-1}u(\rho,t)d\rho, the simplified Keller–Segel system (1.5) can be transformed into a single equation governing its evolution as follows:

Ut=Ur​r+d+1r​Ur+r​Ur​U+d​U2.\displaystyle U_{t}=U_{rr}+\dfrac{d+1}{r}U_{r}+rU_{r}U+dU^{2}.

At the same time, this formulation allows one to make extensive use of comparison principles (see [45, 38, 7]). Moreover, the simplified Keller–Segel system (1.5) and the resulting formulation above exhibits a superlinear structure, which plays a crucial role in the analysis of aggregation and blow-up phenomena.

By contrast, the system (P) remains intrinsically coupled and does not admit a reduction to a single equation nor a superlinear structure. Accordingly, in contrast to the classical setting, the present paper is devoted to clarifying the behavior of the solutions to (P) in the supercritical case. Since the analytical framework available for the simplified Keller–Segel system is not applicable to (P), alternative approaches are required. In this paper, we place particular emphasis on the stationary problem corresponding to (P), which we regard as a key step toward understanding the dynamics of solutions to (P). The associated stationary system reads

{0=Δu−∇⋅(u∇v)in​ℝd×(0,∞),0=Δ​v+win​ℝd×(0,∞),0=Δ​w+uin​ℝd×(0,∞).\begin{cases}0=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)\qquad&\mathrm{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,\infty),\\ 0=\Delta v+w\qquad&\mathrm{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,\infty),\\ 0=\Delta w+u\qquad&\mathrm{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,\infty).\end{cases} (1.6)

By combining the second and third equations, this system is equivalently reduced to the following problem:

{0=Δu−∇⋅(u∇v)in​ℝd×(0,∞),Δ2​v=uin​ℝd×(0,∞).\begin{cases}0=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)\qquad&\mathrm{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,\infty),\\ \Delta^{2}v=u\qquad&\mathrm{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,\infty).\end{cases} (1.7)

Here focusing on the first equation in (1.7), one can rewrite it as ∇⋅(u∇(logu−v))=0\nabla\cdot(u\nabla(\log u-v))=0 in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Hence, if u>0u>0, the stationary problem formally indicates that uu is comparable to eve^{v}. This heuristic relation will be rigorously justified later (see Proposition 6.1). Consequently we consider a radially symmetric solution of the forth-order elliptic problem:

{Δ2​ϕ=eϕfor​r∈[0,R⁡(α,β)),ϕ(0)=logα,Δϕ(0)=β,ϕ′(0)=(Δϕ)′(0)=0,\begin{cases}\Delta^{2}\phi=e^{\phi}\qquad\mathrm{for}\ r\in[0,\mathrm{R}(\alpha,\beta)),\\ \phi(0)=\log\alpha,\ \Delta\phi(0)=\beta,\ \phi^{\prime}(0)=(\Delta\phi)^{\prime}(0)=0,\end{cases} (1.8)

where α>0\alpha>0 and β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R}, and R⁡(α,β)\mathrm{R}(\alpha,\beta) is the maximal interval of existence. Then it is known from [2, 4] that for any α>0\alpha>0 there exists a unique β0(α)∈[−4deα2,0)\beta_{0}(\alpha)\in[-4de^{\frac{\alpha}{2}},0) such that if β=β0​(α)\beta=\beta_{0}(\alpha), then R⁡(α,β)=∞R(\alpha,\beta)=\infty and moreover the corresponding unique radial solution ϕ∈C4​(ℝd)\phi\in C^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfies the following asymptotic profile:

limr→∞(ϕ⁡(r)+4​log⁡r)=log⁡8​(d−4)​(d−2).\displaystyle\lim_{r\to\infty}(\phi(r)+4\log r)=\log 8(d-4)(d-2).

Furthermore, thanks to the refined analysis developed in [21], the asymptotic behavior of the radial solution ϕ\phi near infinity is known in much greater detail. In order to clarify the behavior of solutions to (P) in the supercritical case, we make use of the radially symmetric solution ϕ\phi to the stationary problem (1.8) associated with (P), characterized by the above asymptotic profile.

1.5 Notation

Before stating our main results, we introduce several definitions and remarks that will be used throughout the paper. Throughout the paper, we work with the homogeneous Morrey spaces Mp​(ℝd)M^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) of measurable functions on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, defined by the norm (see [20, Section 7.9]):

‖f‖Mp​(ℝd):=supx∈ℝdsupR>0Rd⁡(1p−1)​∫|x−y|<R|f⁡(y)|​𝑑y<∞.\displaystyle\|f\|_{M^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\sup_{R>0}R^{d(\frac{1}{p}-1)}\int_{|x-y|<R}|f(y)|dy<\infty.

We also set M∞​(ℝd)=L∞​(ℝd)M^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})=L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and M1​(ℝd)=L1​(ℝd)M^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})=L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). In view of the scaling (1.4), the Morrey spaces Md4​(ℝd)M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and Md2​(ℝd)M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) naturally arise as the critical functional framework for the analysis of (P), corresponding to the variables uu and ww, respectively. Moreover, for p∈[1,∞)p\in[1,\infty), we define the subspace M˙p​(ℝd)\dot{M}^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) of Mp​(ℝd)M^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) by

M˙p(ℝd):={f∈Mp(ℝd);lim supR→0Rd⁡(1p−1)∫|x−y|<R|f(y)|dy=0}\displaystyle\dot{M}^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d}):=\{f\in M^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d});\limsup_{R\to 0}R^{d(\frac{1}{p}-1)}\int_{|x-y|<R}|f(y)|dy=0\}

(see [27, 11, 42]). This subspace is essential for constructing local-in-time solutions to (P) in the critical Morrey spaces Md4​(ℝd)M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and Md2​(ℝd)M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Here we basically consider radially symmetric solutions of (P) in this paper. In this case, the norms of the critical Morrey spaces Md4​(ℝd)M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and Md2​(ℝd)M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) are equivalent to

supR>0R4−d​∫|y|<R|f⁡(y)|​𝑑y,supR>0R2−d​∫|y|<R|f⁡(y)|​𝑑y,\displaystyle\sup_{R>0}R^{4-d}\int_{|y|<R}|f(y)|dy,\quad\sup_{R>0}R^{2-d}\int_{|y|<R}|f(y)|dy,

respectively (see [9, Proposition 7.1]). Accordingly, in the radial setting considered in this paper, we shall adopt the above expressions as the definitions of the norms on Md4​(ℝd)M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and Md2​(ℝd)M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Moreover, in the radial setting, the Laplacian of a radially symmetric function f=f⁡(r)f=f(r) is given by

Δ​f​(r):=fr​r​(r)+d−1r​fr​(r).\displaystyle\Delta f(r):=f_{rr}(r)+\dfrac{d-1}{r}f_{r}(r).

As usual, by the Taylor expansion, the value at the origin is defined by Δ​f​(0):=d​fr​r​(0)\Delta f(0):=df_{rr}(0). Finally, we note that there are several natural ways to treat the second equation in (P), which is of Poisson type. One approach is to assume that vv is given by the convolution

v=Ed∗w,\displaystyle v=E_{d}*w,

where EdE_{d} denotes the fundamental solution of the Laplacian, given by

Ed​(x)=1(d−2)​σd​1|x|d−2for​d≥3,\displaystyle E_{d}(x)=\dfrac{1}{(d-2)\sigma_{d}}\dfrac{1}{|x|^{d-2}}\quad\mathrm{for}\ d\geq 3,

where σd\sigma_{d} is the measure of the unit sphere in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. A second approach is to take advantage of radial symmetry and define vv by an integral formula:

v(x,t):=−∫0|x|s1−d∫0sρd−1w(ρ,t)dρds+Cfor(x,t)∈ℝd×(0,∞)\displaystyle v(x,t):=-\int_{0}^{|x|}s^{1-d}\int_{0}^{s}\rho^{d-1}w(\rho,t)d\rho ds+C\quad\mathrm{for}\ (x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,\infty) (1.9)

with some constant CC. We also denote the radial inverse of the Laplacian (−Δ)−1(-\Delta)^{-1} by the following integral form

(−Δ)−1f(x):=−∫0|x|s1−d∫0sρd−1f(ρ)dρdsforx∈ℝd∖{0}\displaystyle(-\Delta)^{-1}f(x):=-\int_{0}^{|x|}s^{1-d}\int_{0}^{s}\rho^{d-1}f(\rho)d\rho ds\quad\mathrm{for}\ x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\}

and extend it to r=0r=0 by continuity, so that (−Δ)−1​f​(0)=0(-\Delta)^{-1}f(0)=0. Throughout this paper, we shall employ these two definitions selectively, according to the requirements of each theorem.

1.6 Main results

Our main results are stated as follows.

Theorem 1.1 (Singular stationary solutions).

Let d≥7d\geq 7 and

uC​(x)=8​(d−4)​(d−2)|x|4,wC​(x)=4​(d−2)|x|2,vC​(x)=−4​log⁡|x|+C\displaystyle u_{C}(x)=\dfrac{8(d-4)(d-2)}{|x|^{4}},\quad w_{C}(x)=\dfrac{4(d-2)}{|x|^{2}},\quad v_{C}(x)=-4\log|x|+C

for some constant CC. Then (uC,vC,wC)(u_{C},v_{C},w_{C}) is a distributional, stationary solution to the system (P).

Remark 1.2.

This stands in sharp contrast to the simplified Keller–Segel system (1.5), whose singular stationary state is generated by the Chandrasekhar steady state singular solution |x|−2|x|^{-2}. Hence, our system admits a fundamentally different type of singular structure, that the dynamics of our system may display novel features that cannot appear in the theory of the classical Keller–Segel systems.

Let us present the result on the global-in-time solutions to the system (P).

Theorem 1.3.

Let d≥5d\geq 5 and let p∈(d3,d2)p\in(\frac{d}{3},\frac{d}{2}) be close to d3\frac{d}{3}. Assume the radially symmetric nonnegative initial data (u0,w0)∈(Md4​(ℝd)∩M˙p​(ℝd))×(Md2​(ℝd)∩Md​pd−2​p​(ℝd))(u_{0},w_{0})\in(M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap\dot{M}^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))\times(M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap M^{\frac{dp}{d-2p}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})) satisfying

‖u0‖Md4​(ℝd)\displaystyle\|u_{0}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})} :=supR>0R4−d​∫|x|<Ru0​(x)​𝑑x<6​(d−2)​σd,\displaystyle:=\sup_{R>0}R^{4-d}\int_{|x|<R}u_{0}(x)dx<6(d-2)\sigma_{d}, (1.10)
‖w0‖Md2​(ℝd)\displaystyle\|w_{0}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})} :=supR>0R2−d​∫|x|<Rw0​(x)​𝑑x<3​σd.\displaystyle:=\sup_{R>0}R^{2-d}\int_{|x|<R}w_{0}(x)dx<3\sigma_{d}. (1.11)

Then the corresponding solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) to the problem (P) exists globally in time in the sense

Remark 1.4.

The straightforwrd computation implies

‖uC‖Md4​(ℝd)=8​(d−2)​σd,‖wC‖Md2​(ℝd)=4​σd.\displaystyle\|u_{C}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=8(d-2)\sigma_{d},\quad\|w_{C}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=4\sigma_{d}.

Therefore, in view of the result [7] known for the simplified Keller–Segel system (1.5), the conclusion of Theorem 1.3 can be regarded as weaker than the expected optimal statement for (P), which would assert global-in-time existence together with the same bounds under natural assumptions. More precisely, we expect under the assumption

‖u0‖Md4​(ℝd)<‖uC‖Md4​(ℝd)=8​(d−2)​σd,‖w0‖Md2​(ℝd)<‖wC‖Md2​(ℝd)=4​σd,\displaystyle\|u_{0}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}<\|u_{C}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=8(d-2)\sigma_{d},\quad\|w_{0}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}<\|w_{C}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=4\sigma_{d}, (1.13)

the corresponding solution to (P), defined in an appropriate functional setting, exists globally in time and enjoys the same bounds. Hence Theorem 1.3 does not yet reach this level and is weaker in this respect. Nevertheless, such a result in the supercritical case for an essentially parabolic-parabolic system (P) is completely new.

Focusing on the radial solution ϕ\phi of (1.8), we construct both global-in-time solutions and finite time blow-up of solutions.

Let ϕ∈C4​(ℝd)\phi\in C^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be the radial solution of (1.8) with α>0\alpha>0 and β0​(α)\beta_{0}(\alpha) and assume the radially symmetric nonnegative initial data (u0,w0)∈(C⁡(ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd))2(u_{0},w_{0})\in(C(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))^{2}. Remark 1.6.

The local-in-time existence of a solution to (P) corresponding to the initial data (u0,w0)∈(C⁡(ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd))2(u_{0},w_{0})\in(C(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))^{2} is guaranteed by Proposition 3.8. Especially the function vv is denoted by the integral formula (1.9).

Remark 1.7.

For the radially symmetric solution ϕ\phi of the elliptic problem (1.8) associated with the parameters α\alpha and β0​(α)\beta_{0}(\alpha), the functions eϕe^{\phi} and (−Δ)​ϕ(-\Delta)\phi are asymptotic to the singular stationary solutions uCu_{C} and wCw_{C}, respectively, as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty (see [21, 2, 4] and Section 6). Consequently Theorem 1.5 highlights that the long-time behavior in supercritical dimensions of solutions to (P) is governed by whether the initial data (u0,w0)(u_{0},w_{0}) lies above or below these singular profiles at infinity.

Thanks to Theorem 1.5, we obtain the following result. The following theorems yield an essentially complete classification for the behavior of the solutions to (P) in supercritical dimensions.

Theorem 1.8.

Let ϕ∈C4​(ℝd)\phi\in C^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be the radial solution of (1.8) with α>0\alpha>0 and β0​(α)\beta_{0}(\alpha) and assume the radially symmetric nonnegative initial data (u0,w0)∈(C⁡(ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd))2(u_{0},w_{0})\in(C(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))^{2}. Then the following two assertions hold.

    If d≥13d\geq 13, whenever the initial data (u0,w0)(u_{0},w_{0}) satisfies

    0≤u0≤eϕ,0≤w0≤(−Δ)​ϕfor​all​x∈ℝd,\displaystyle 0\leq u_{0}\leq e^{\phi},\quad 0\leq w_{0}\leq(-\Delta)\phi\quad\mathrm{for\ all}\ x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

    supt>0‖u⁡(t)‖Md4​(ℝd)≤8​(d−2)​σd,supt>0‖w⁡(t)‖Md2​(ℝd)≤4​σd.\displaystyle\sup_{t>0}\|u(t)\|_{M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq 8(d-2)\sigma_{d},\quad\sup_{t>0}\|w(t)\|_{M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq 4\sigma_{d}. (1.15)
  2. (ii)

    If 5≤d≤125\leq d\leq 12, then there exists λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1) such that, whenever the initial data (u0,w0)(u_{0},w_{0}) satisfies

    0≤u0≤λ​eϕ,0≤w0≤λ⁡(−Δ)​ϕfor​all​x∈ℝd,\displaystyle 0\leq u_{0}\leq\lambda e^{\phi},\quad 0\leq w_{0}\leq\lambda(-\Delta)\phi\quad\mathrm{for\ all}\ x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

Remark 1.9.

In the case d≥13d\geq 13, the critical Morrey norms of eϕe^{\phi} and (−Δ)​ϕ(-\Delta)\phi coincide with the critical values, namely,

‖eϕ‖Md4​(ℝd)=8​(d−2)​σd,‖(−Δ)​ϕ‖Md2​(ℝd)=4​σd\displaystyle\|e^{\phi}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=8(d-2)\sigma_{d},\quad\|(-\Delta)\phi\|_{M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=4\sigma_{d}

as proved in Lemma 8.1. Hence the assumption in Theorem 1.8 (i) is sufficient to ensure that

‖u0‖Md4​(ℝd)≤8​(d−2)​σd,‖w0‖Md2​(ℝd)≤4​σd.\displaystyle\|u_{0}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq 8(d-2)\sigma_{d},\quad\|w_{0}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq 4\sigma_{d}. (1.16)

Moreover, when 5≤d≤125\leq d\leq 12, the above condition can still be achieved by choosing a suitable value of λ\lambda. Therefore this observation suggests that the initial assumptions (1.10) and (1.11) in Theorem 1.3 might be extendable to the condition (1.16) which includes the limiting case in (1.13).

Finally, we present the following result concerning large initial data.

Theorem 1.10.

The following two statements are valid.

  1. (i)

    Let d≥13d\geq 13 and K0>8​(d−2)​σdK_{0}>8(d-2)\sigma_{d}, and K1>4​σdK_{1}>4\sigma_{d}. Then there exists (u0,w0)∈(C⁡(ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd))2(u_{0},w_{0})\in(C(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))^{2} such that

    ‖u0‖Md4​(ℝd)=K0,‖w0‖Md2​(ℝd)=K1\displaystyle\|u_{0}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=K_{0},\quad\|w_{0}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=K_{1}

    and the corresponding solution blows up in finite time.

  2. (ii)

    Let 5≤d≤125\leq d\leq 12. Then there exists (u0,w0)∈(C⁡(ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd))2(u_{0},w_{0})\in(C(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))^{2} such that

    ‖u0‖Md4​(ℝd)>8​(d−2)​σd,‖w0‖Md2​(ℝd)>4​σd\displaystyle\|u_{0}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}>8(d-2)\sigma_{d},\quad\|w_{0}\|_{M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}>4\sigma_{d}

    and the corresponding solution exists globally in time.

Remark 1.11.

Theorem 1.10 shows that, for d≥13d\geq 13, the values 8​(d−2)​σd8(d-2)\sigma_{d} and 4​σd4\sigma_{d} serve as critical thresholds in the corresponding Morrey spaces, across which the long-time behavior of solutions to (P) changes. In this sense, these values are optimal. On the other hand, when 5≤d≤125\leq d\leq 12, the situation is different in this respect. Therefore, it appears highly interesting to investigate the long-time behavior of solutions in this dimensional range.

Remark 1.12.

For the essentially parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis system (P), Theorem 1.8 and Theorem 1.10, which yield a sharp criterion and a complete classification of global existence and finite time blow-up of solutions, have not been previously available. Therefore, our approach and results of the present paper are expected to be of independent interest.

1.7 Strategy and plan of the paper

The main strategy and the plan of this paper are summarized as follows. A central difficulty in the analysis of system (P) lies in the fact that, unlike the classical parabolic-elliptic Keller–Segel system (1.5), it does not reduce to a single equation nor possess an explicit superlinear structure. As a consequence, many techniques developed for the Keller–Segel system cannot be applied directly.

To overcome this difficulty, we introduce and exploit new comparison principles for the radial version of the original system (P), together with suitably defined mass functions (2.6) and (2.7) associated with (P). These comparison principles, developed in Section 2, form a key analytical tool. More precisely, the comparison principle established for the original system (P) allows us to construct local-in-time solutions from the initial data (u0,w0)∈(C⁡(ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd))2(u_{0},w_{0})\in(C(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))^{2}. In contrast, the comparison principle for the associated mass functions serves as a key ingredient in controlling the dynamical behavior of solutions to the system (2.8) for the mass function.

In Section 3, we establish local-in-time existence of solutions to (P) in appropriate function spaces. As a first step, we construct local-in-time solutions with v=Ed∗wv=E_{d}*w in the scaling-critical Morrey spaces. Such solutions are obtained by a standard application of the Banach fixed point theorem (see [7, 11, 17, 24]). As a second approach, we construct the solutions using the comparison principle established in Section 2 and radial symmetry. In this case, the potential vv is expressed through a radial integral representation (1.9).

In Section 4, we present the proofs of Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.3. In particular, the proof of Theorem 1.3 is inspired by the approach developed in [7]. However, since the system under consideration is essentially of parabolic-parabolic type, consisting of two genuinely coupled equations, additional care is required to adapt this method to the present setting.

In Section 5, we develop the analytical framework needed to prove convergence of solutions toward the stationary state. However, we cannot rely on arguments based on the parabolic-elliptic structure of the simplified Keller–Segel system (1.5) (see [45, 38]). Instead, we construct a novel subsolution to the system (2.8) satisfied by the mass functions that exhibits finite time blow-up. This approach enables us to prove that infinite time blow-up can occur only at the origin, which in turn leads to convergence of the mass functions toward the stationary state. We stress that the novelty of our approach lies not only in the construction of a new blowing up subsolution itself, but also in the strategy behind its construction, which may have further applications to other nonlinear parabolic systems beyond the classical Keller–Segel system.

In Section 6, we investigate the convergence toward stationary solutions and their qualitative properties. We first show that the stationary problem (1.6) associated with (P) coincides with the forth-order elliptic problem (1.8). This fact, together with the assumptions of Theorem 1.5, allows the comparison principles developed earlier to be applied effectively in the proof of Theorem 1.5 (see the next section). Next, we establish convergence of the mass functions toward their stationary states. After that, starting from the stationary mass functions, we construct the corresponding stationary solutions to the original system (P). Unlike approaches that focus primarily on the stationary mass function (see [45, 38]), we place particular emphasis on the analysis of the asymptotic behavior of stationary solutions to the original problem (P). This constitutes a new perspective in the study of the system.

In Section 7, we provide the proof of Theorem 1.5 based on the results established in the preceding sections. A key point of the argument is that the proof relies on a detailed analysis of the stationary solutions to the original problem (P), rather than on the stationary problem for the mass functions.

Finally, in Section 8, motivated by the results [21, 4] showing that the asymptotic behavior of radially symmetric solutions to (1.8) depends on the space dimension, we present the proofs of Theorem 1.8 and Theorem 1.10.

2 Comparison principles

In this section, we develop the comparison principles that serve as a fundamental tool in proving the main theorems of this paper. The first comparison principle is formulated directly for the original system (P). In particular, it allows us to construct ODE–type subsolutions and supersolutions to (P), which will play a crucial role in the proof of Proposition 3.8.

3 Local-in-time solutions

In this section, we begin by introducing local existence of classical solutions to (P) and provide two approaches to the construction of solutions. The first one is based on representing v=Ed∗wv=E_{d}*w by the Newtonian potential, which is particularly useful for establishing Theorem 1.3. The second approach relies on exploiting radial symmetry without using the Newtonian representation of vv. This second construction provides the regularity properties required in the analysis of Theorem 1.5 and Theorem 1.8, and Theorem 1.10. To verify the first existence result, we establish several auxiliary lemmas.

Lemma 3.1 ([19, Proposition 3.2]).

Let (et​Δ)t≥0(e^{t\Delta})_{t\geq 0} be the heat semigroup on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Then there exists C>0C>0 independent of t>0t>0 such that for all 1≤p≤q≤∞1\leq p\leq q\leq\infty

Let d≥5d\geq 5 and p∈(d3,d2)p\in(\frac{d}{3},\frac{d}{2}). w∈Cw​([0,T],Md2​(ℝd)∩Md​pd−2​p​(ℝd)),\displaystyle w\in C_{w}([0,T];M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap M^{\frac{dp}{d-2p}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})),

Remark 3.4.

The assumptions of the parameters pp and rr ensure that

r<d<d​pd−2​p.\displaystyle r<d<\dfrac{dp}{d-2p}.

This condition is essential in establishing a local-in-time solution via the Banach fixed-point argument.

Remark 3.5.

In view of [11] and [27, Lemma 2.2], the membership u0∈M˙p​(ℝd)u_{0}\in\dot{M}^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is a necessary condition for constructing a local-in-time solution to (P) in the critical Morrey space. Indeed, when u0∈M˙p​(ℝd)u_{0}\in\dot{M}^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) it holds that

limt→0td2​(1p−1r)​‖et​Δ​u0‖Mr​(ℝd)=0.\displaystyle\lim_{t\to 0}t^{\frac{d}{2}(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{r})}\|e^{t\Delta}u_{0}\|_{M^{r}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=0.

Hence, by choosing T>0T>0 sufficiently small, this term can be made arbitrarily small and therefore controlled within the fixed point framework.

Remark 3.6.

As pointed out in [27, Section 2 and Lemma 3.1], one generally obtains only weak convergence of et​Δ​u0e^{t\Delta}u_{0} and et​Δ​w0e^{t\Delta}w_{0} when u0∈Md4​(ℝd)u_{0}\in M^{\frac{d}{4}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and w0∈Md2​(ℝd)w_{0}\in M^{\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). However, for every t>0t>0 the heat semigroup is strongly continuous in the corresponding Morrey norms. Moreover we can confirm that the mild solution established by Proposition 3.3 can be shown to extend to a nonnegative classical solution for all t>0t>0, by employing the iteration method developed in [42] and the parabolic maximum principle.

Proof..

By the argument in the proof of Proposition 3.3 combination with [44, Lemma 2.1], we can construct a mild solution on a short time interval. Moreover, the continuity at t=0t=0 is guaranteed by the fact that the heat semigroup preserves pointwise continuity at t=0t=0 when (u0,w0)∈(C⁡(ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd))2(u_{0},w_{0})\in(C(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))^{2} (see [32]). The nonnegativity of the solution follows from the parabolic maximum principle together with the nonnegativity of the initial data. ∎

4 Proof of Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.3

In what follows, we emphasize that the fundamental problem we face for the system (P) is to identify the critical quantity or, more precisely, the explicit function that determines the long-time behavior of its solutions. We first point out that the problem is deeply related to stationary, radial, and homogeneous solutions of the system (P). Since the system (P) is invariant by a standard scaling argument, any such stationary profile must necessarily be a multiple of |x|α|x|^{\alpha}. Motivated by this observation, we perform a formal computation to determine the constant appearing in such stationary profiles and thereby introduce a new singular stationary solution.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

By a scaling argument, we may look for stationary solutions of the form

u=A|x|4,v=C​log⁡|x|+C0,w=B|x|2\displaystyle u=\frac{A}{|x|^{4}},\quad v=C\log|x|+C_{0},\quad w=\frac{B}{|x|^{2}}

for some constants A,B,C,C0A,B,C,C_{0}. These functions are understood to satisfy the stationary problem (1.6) associated with (P) in the sense of distributions. Throughout the following computations, all identities are to be interpreted in the distributional sense. The third equation of (1.6) implies that

B⁡(2​d−8)|x|4=A|x|4\displaystyle\dfrac{B(2d-8)}{|x|^{4}}=\dfrac{A}{|x|^{4}} (4.1)

and we rewrite the second equation as

C⁡(2−d)|x|2=B|x|2.\displaystyle\dfrac{C(2-d)}{|x|^{2}}=\dfrac{B}{|x|^{2}}. (4.2)

Moreover it readily from the first equation of (1.6) that

0=−A​(4+C)​(d−6)|x|6,\displaystyle 0=\dfrac{-A(4+C)(d-6)}{|x|^{6}},

which means that for every d≥7d\geq 7 we must have −A⁡(4+C)=0-A(4+C)=0. Combing this fact with (4.1) and (4.2), we conclude that

A=8​(d−4)​(d−2),B=4​(d−2),C=−4.\displaystyle A=8(d-4)(d-2),\quad B=4(d-2),\quad C=-4.

We emphasize that the condition d≥7d\geq 7 is not only required for the above algebraic argument, but is also essential to ensure that the corresponding singular stationary solution satisfies (1.6) in the sense of distributions. Indeed for the singular profile uC∼r−4u_{C}\sim r^{-4} and (vC)r∼r−1(v_{C})_{r}\sim r^{-1}, the chemotactic flux term satisfies

∇⋅(uC∇vC)=r1−d(rd−1uC(vC)r)r∼r1−d(rd−6)r.\displaystyle\nabla\cdot(u_{C}\nabla v_{C})=r^{1-d}(r^{d-1}u_{C}(v_{C})_{r})_{r}\sim r^{1-d}(r^{d-6})_{r}.

Thus the requirement d≥7d\geq 7 is necessary to ensure that the chemotactic flux term uC∇vCu_{C}\nabla v_{C} is locally integrable and that the equation holds in the distributional sense. ∎

We now proceed to provide a rigorous proof of Theorem 1.3. In order to rigorously establish Theorem 1.3, we make use of a specially designed mass function, distinct from (2.6) and (2.7), that turns out to be a fundamental tool in the forthcoming argument (see [8, 9, 7, 6]). The simplified Keller–Segel system (1.5) can be reduced to a scalar parabolic problem through an appropriate change of variables. In contrast, our system (P) admits no such reduction and therefore truly remains a coupled system. Assume that (u,v,w)(u,v,w) is a radially symmetric solution classically in ℝd×(0,T)\mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,T), obtained in Proposition 3.3. We introduce the mass function (X,Y)(X,Y) by

X⁡(r,t)\displaystyle X(r,t) :=∫|x|<ru⁡(x,t)​𝑑x=σd​∫0rρd−1​u​(ρ,t)​𝑑ρ,\displaystyle:=\int_{|x|<r}u(x,t)dx=\sigma_{d}\int_{0}^{r}\rho^{d-1}u(\rho,t)d\rho, (4.3)
Y⁡(r,t)\displaystyle Y(r,t) :=∫|x|<rw⁡(x,t)​𝑑x\displaystyle:=\int_{|x|<r}w(x,t)dx (4.4)

for all (r,t)∈(0,∞)×[0,T)(r,t)\in(0,\infty)\times[0,T), where we impose the natural conditions

X⁡(0,t)=0,Y⁡(0,t)=0for​t∈[0,T).\displaystyle X(0,t)=0,\quad Y(0,t)=0\quad\mathrm{for}\ t\in[0,T).

Then (X,Y)(X,Y) belongs to [C1​([0,∞)×[0,T))∩C2,1​((0,∞)×(0,T))]2[C^{1}([0,\infty)\times[0,T))\cap C^{2,1}((0,\infty)\times(0,T))]^{2} satisfying the system

{Xt=Xr​r−d−1r​Xr+1σd​r1−d​Xr​Yin⁡(0,∞)×(0,T),Yt=Yr​r−d−1r​Yr+Xin⁡(0,∞)×(0,T).\begin{cases}X_{t}=X_{rr}-\dfrac{d-1}{r}X_{r}+\dfrac{1}{\sigma_{d}}r^{1-d}X_{r}Y\qquad&\mathrm{in}\ (0,\infty)\times(0,T),\\ Y_{t}=Y_{rr}-\dfrac{d-1}{r}Y_{r}+X\qquad&\mathrm{in}\ (0,\infty)\times(0,T).\end{cases} (4.5)

In the study [7] on the simplified Keller–Segel system (1.5), the elliptic equation enables a further reduction to a single equation, and the coupling term Xr​YX_{r}Y in the first equation of (4.5) is replaced by the quadratic term Xr​XX_{r}X. The proof of the next proposition is inspired by [7, Proposition 4.1]. However, it is important to stress that our analysis is carried out for the system (4.5).

5 The existence of blow up points at infinite time via Comparison Principles

In this section, we develop the arguments required to establish convergence toward the stationary state. For the simplified Keller–Segel system (1.5), the second equation reduces to the Poisson equation, and by utilizing the radial symmetry and the corresponding mass function, the system can essentially be rewritten as a single equation. This structure allows one to exploit suitable test functions to derive superlinear inequalities for certain energy type quantities, leading to Kaplan-type blow-up arguments (see [26, 45, 38]). As a consequence, it can be shown that blow-up may occur only at the origin, which in turn enables the analysis of convergence to stationary solutions away from the singularity. In contrast, the parabolic system (2.8) derived from (P) is genuinely coupled and cannot be reduced to a single parabolic equation. Hence the aforementioned techniques are not directly applicable. Therefore, in this section we rely on the comparison principle developed in Chapter 2 to locate the possible blow-up point and to prepare the analysis required for convergence to stationary solutions. Here we make use of the monotonicity of (M,W)(M,W) for r>0r>0.

Assume that (u,v,w)(u,v,w) is the solution of (P) in ℝd×(0,T)\mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,T) given by Proposition 3.8. 6 Stationary Problems and Convergence Properties of solutions

In this section, we investigate the properties of stationary solutions to the original system (P), and subsequently analyze the convergence of solutions to the system (2.8) for the mass function toward such stationary states. We begin by showing that the stationary solution to (P) necessarily coincides with a solution of the fourth-order elliptic problem (1.8). This reveals a precise correspondence between steady states of (P) and those of the biharmonic Gel’fand problem.

Proposition 6.1.

Let d≥5d\geq 5 and α>0\alpha>0, and β0(α)∈[−4dα12,0)\beta_{0}(\alpha)\in[-4d\alpha^{\frac{1}{2}},0). Then the following two assertions are equivalent.

    the radially symmetric pair (u,v)(u,v), with u>0u>0 everywhere, solves (1.7) in the classical sense in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and satisfies the following conditions:

    (u,v)​(0)=(α,log⁡α),Δ​v​(0)=β0​(α),v′​(0)=(Δ​v)′​(0)=0.\displaystyle(u,v)(0)=(\alpha,\log\alpha),\quad\Delta v(0)=\beta_{0}(\alpha),\quad v^{\prime}(0)=(\Delta v)^{\prime}(0)=0.
  2. (ii)

    the functions uu and vv are given by eϕe^{\phi} and ϕ\phi respectively, where the radially symmetric function ϕ∈C4​(ℝd)\phi\in C^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) solves (1.8) in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with ϕ⁡(0)=log⁡α\phi(0)=\log\alpha and Δ​ϕ​(0)=β0​(α)\Delta\phi(0)=\beta_{0}(\alpha).

Moreover, any solution of (1.7) satisfying the conditions above is radially decreasing and also enjoys the property

∇⋅(u∇v)<0inℝd,\displaystyle\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)<0\quad\mathrm{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{d}, (6.1)

and moreover setting w=−Δ​vw=-\Delta v yields a positive, radially decreasing function ww with

lim|x|→∞w⁡(x)=0.\displaystyle\lim_{|x|\to\infty}w(x)=0. (6.2)

The fact that the sign of the advective term is completely determined by the inequality (6.1) is highly significant. This observation plays a crucial role in the subsequent analysis. Indeed, once the sign is identified, it enables us to construct suitable functions satisfying subsolution or supersolution properties for (2.8).

We now assume (i). Multiplying the radial version of the first equation in (1.7) by rd−1r^{d-1} and integrating it over (0,r)(0,r), we have

7 Proof of Theorem 1.5

In what follows, we give a rigorous proof of Theorem 1.5. Although the previous section established the stationary solution (M∞,W∞)(M_{\infty},W_{\infty}) for the mass function formulation (2.8) and then constructed the associated stationary solution (u∞,v∞,w∞)(u_{\infty},v_{\infty},w_{\infty}) of the original system (P), the analysis required for Theorem 1.5 depends essentially on the full stationary structure of the original system (P). Our approach highlights that the key ingredient lies in the asymptotic analysis of the original stationary solution (u∞,v∞,w∞)(u_{\infty},v_{\infty},w_{\infty}). This perspective appears to be novel and provides a deeper structural understanding of the system (P).

Proposition 7.1.

Let r0≥0r_{0}\geq 0 and d≥5d\geq 5. Assume that (u,v,w)(u,v,w) is a radially symmetric solution, with uu and ww nonnegative in r>r0r>r_{0}, to

The assumption (7.2) in Proposition 7.1 is reasonable in view of the conclusion obtained in [2, 4]. More precisely, in [2, Theorem 2] and [4, Theorem 4] it is shown that when d≥5d\geq 5, then for any α>0\alpha>0 there is a unique parameter β0∈[−4dα12,0)\beta_{0}\in[-4d\alpha^{\frac{1}{2}},0) such that the corresponding solution ϕα,β0∈C4​((0,∞))\phi_{\alpha,\beta_{0}}\in C^{4}((0,\infty)) of (1.8) satisfies the asymptotic profile

limr→∞(ϕα,β0​(r)+4​log⁡r)=log⁡8​(d−4)​(d−2).\displaystyle\lim_{r\to\infty}(\phi_{\alpha,\beta_{0}}(r)+4\log r)=\log 8(d-4)(d-2).

On the other hand, it is also proved that if β<β0\beta<\beta_{0}, then the solution ϕα,β∈C4​((0,∞))\phi_{\alpha,\beta}\in C^{4}((0,\infty)) of (1.8) enjoys the upper estimate

ϕα,β​(r)≤α−β0−β2​d​r2for​all​r∈[0,∞).\displaystyle\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(r)\leq\alpha-\dfrac{\beta_{0}-\beta}{2d}r^{2}\quad\mathrm{for\ all}\ r\in[0,\infty).

Hence the validity of the asymptotic profile depends crucially on the choice of β\beta. Consequently, our assumption expresses precisely the condition under which the expected asymptotic behavior holds.

Proof of Theorem 1.5.

(i) Let T>0T>0 and (u,v,w)(u,v,w) be a radially symmetric solution of (P) in ℝd×(0,T)\mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,T), where uu and ww are nonnegative. Let (M,W)(M,W) denote the associated mass function defined by (2.6) and (2.7). Owing to these definitions, the identity holds that

r​Mr+d​M=r1−d​(rd​M)r=u≥0for​all​(r,t)∈(0,∞)×(0,T).\displaystyle rM_{r}+dM=r^{1-d}(r^{d}M)_{r}=u\geq 0\quad\mathrm{for\ all}\ (r,t)\in(0,\infty)\times(0,T).

Here we note that (λ​eϕ,λ⁡(−Δ)​ϕ)(\lambda e^{\phi},\lambda(-\Delta)\phi) is radially nonincreasing (see Proposition 6.1) and is regular at the origin, and also decays to zero at infinity. Therefore, when (λ​eϕ,λ⁡(−Δ)​ϕ)(\lambda e^{\phi},\lambda(-\Delta)\phi) is taken as initial data, Proposition 3.8 ensures the existence of a corresponding solution to (P). Moreover since (λ​eϕ,λ⁡(−Δ)​ϕ)(\lambda e^{\phi},\lambda(-\Delta)\phi) satisfies (3.11), one can check that the mass functions generated by (λ​eϕ,λ⁡(−Δ)​ϕ)(\lambda e^{\phi},\lambda(-\Delta)\phi) inherit the supersolution property of the system (2.8). Therefore, since all the assumptions of Lemma 2.2 are satisfied for solutions generated by Proposition 3.8, we may invoke Lemma 2.2 to obtain, for all (r,t)∈[0,∞)×[0,T)(r,t)\in[0,\infty)\times[0,T),

M⁡(r,t)\displaystyle M(r,t) ≤λ​r−d​∫0rρd−1​eϕ​𝑑ρ,\displaystyle\leq\lambda r^{-d}\int_{0}^{r}\rho^{d-1}e^{\phi}d\rho,

Consequently we conclude that the solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) exists globally in time and enjoys the upper bound (1.14).

(ii) Let T>0T>0 and (u,v,w)(u,v,w) be a radially symmetric solution of (P) in ℝd×(0,T)\mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,T), where uu and ww are nonnegative. Hence owing to the monotonicity in t>0t>0 for (Mλ,Wλ)(M_{\lambda},W_{\lambda}), Proposition 6.4 enables us to get the limit function (Mλ,∞,Wλ,∞)∈[C2​((0,∞))∩L∞​(r0,∞)]2(M_{\lambda,\infty},W_{\lambda,\infty})\in[C^{2}((0,\infty))\cap L^{\infty}(r_{0},\infty)]^{2} for any r0>0r_{0}>0 satisfying (6.6) and moreover,

r​(Mλ,∞)r+d​Mλ,∞≥0for​r∈(0,∞).\displaystyle r(M_{\lambda,\infty})_{r}+dM_{\lambda,\infty}\geq 0\quad\mathrm{for}\ r\in(0,\infty). (7.12)

Mλ,0​(r)≤Mλ​(r,t)≤Mλ,∞​(r),Wλ,0​(r)≤Wλ​(r,t)≤Wλ,∞​(r).\displaystyle M_{\lambda,0}(r)\leq M_{\lambda}(r,t)\leq M_{\lambda,\infty}(r),\quad W_{\lambda,0}(r)\leq W_{\lambda}(r,t)\leq W_{\lambda,\infty}(r). (7.13)

as well as

(iii) Since λ1>λ2>1\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}>1, the proof of (ii) extends directly, by Proposition 6.3. ∎

8 Proof of Theorem 1.8 and Theorem 1.10

In this section, motivated by the results obtained in [2, 4], we demonstrate that the qualitative behavior of solutions to the system (P) changes depending on the spatial dimension. Our approach is to focus first on the radial solution of the fourth-order elliptic problem (1.8) and to show that the Morrey norms for (eϕ,(−Δ)​ϕ)(e^{\phi},(-\Delta)\phi) differ significantly with the dimension.

Lemma 8.1.

Let d≥13d\geq 13 and ϕ∈C4​(ℝd)\phi\in C^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be a radially symmetric solution of (1.8) with initial conditions

ϕ⁡(0)=log⁡α,Δ​ϕ​(0)=β0​(α),ϕ′​(0)=(Δ​ϕ)′​(0)=0,\displaystyle\phi(0)=\log\alpha,\quad\Delta\phi(0)=\beta_{0}(\alpha),\quad\phi^{\prime}(0)=(\Delta\phi)^{\prime}(0)=0,

where α>0\alpha>0 and β0(α)∈[−4dα12,0)\beta_{0}(\alpha)\in[-4d\alpha^{\frac{1}{2}},0). Then it holds that

supR>0R4−d​∫0Rrd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r=8​(d−2)\displaystyle\sup_{R>0}R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr=8(d-2) (8.1)

as well as

supR>0R2−d​∫0Rrd−1​(−Δ)​ϕ​(r)​𝑑r=4.\displaystyle\sup_{R>0}R^{2-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}(-\Delta)\phi(r)dr=4. (8.2)
Proof..

According to [4, Lemma 12], when d≥13d\geq 13, the regular radial solution ϕ\phi of (1.8) with the prescribed conditions at the origin and a singular radial solution −4​log⁡r+log⁡8​(d−4)​(d−2)-4\log r+\log 8(d-4)(d-2) of (1.8) do not intersect each other for r>0r>0, namely we have

ϕ⁡(r)<log⁡8​(d−4)​(d−2)r4for​r∈(0,∞).\displaystyle\phi(r)<\log\dfrac{8(d-4)(d-2)}{r^{4}}\quad\mathrm{for}\ r\in(0,\infty). (8.3)

This behavior implies that for R>0R>0

R4−d​∫0Rrd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r\displaystyle R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr <R4−d​∫0Rrd−1​8​(d−4)​(d−2)r4​𝑑r=8​(d−2).\displaystyle<R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}\dfrac{8(d-4)(d-2)}{r^{4}}dr=8(d-2). (8.4)

On the other hand, the asymptotic behavior of ϕ\phi in light of [2, Theorem 2] and [4, Theorem 4]:

ϕ⁡(r)=−4​log⁡r+log⁡8​(d−4)​(d−2)+o⁡(1)as​r→∞\displaystyle\phi(r)=-4\log r+\log 8(d-4)(d-2)+o(1)\quad\mathrm{as}\ r\to\infty

immediately implies that ∫0Rrd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r→∞\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr\to\infty as R→∞R\to\infty, allowing the use of L’Hospital’s rule. Consequently we get

limR→∞R4−d​∫0Rrd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r\displaystyle\lim_{R\to\infty}R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr =limR→∞Rd−1​eϕ⁡(R)(d−4)​Rd−5=8​(d−2),\displaystyle=\lim_{R\to\infty}\dfrac{R^{d-1}e^{\phi(R)}}{(d-4)R^{d-5}}=8(d-2),

which lead to our desired conclusion (8.1) together with (8.4). We next confirm (8.2). Since the solution ϕ\phi solves the fourth-order equation Δ2​ϕ=eϕ\Delta^{2}\phi=e^{\phi} on [0,∞)[0,\infty), the result in [21, Theorem 1.1] leads to the following estimate:

−Δ​ϕ​(r)<4​(d−2)r2for​all​r∈(0,∞).\displaystyle-\Delta\phi(r)<\dfrac{4(d-2)}{r^{2}}\quad\mathrm{for\ all}\ r\in(0,\infty).

Hence we obtain for any R>0R>0

R2−d​∫0Rrd−1​(−Δ)​ϕ​(r)​𝑑r<4​(d−2)​R2−d​∫0Rrd−3​𝑑r=4.\displaystyle R^{2-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}(-\Delta)\phi(r)dr<4(d-2)R^{2-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-3}dr=4.

Moreover as noted in the proof (see (6.5)) in Proposition 6.1, the detailed asymptotic expansion of ϕ\phi is available thanks to the results in [21]. This allows us to apply L’Hospital’s rule to deduce

limR→∞R2−d​∫0Rrd−1​(−Δ)​ϕ​(r)​𝑑r=limR→∞Rd−1​(−Δ)​ϕ​(R)(d−2)​Rd−3=4,\displaystyle\lim_{R\to\infty}R^{2-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}(-\Delta)\phi(r)dr=\lim_{R\to\infty}\dfrac{R^{d-1}(-\Delta)\phi(R)}{(d-2)R^{d-3}}=4,

which clearly proves (8.2). ∎

Lemma 8.2.

Let 5≤d≤125\leq d\leq 12 and let ϕ∈C4​(ℝd)\phi\in C^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be a radially symmetric solution of (1.8) with the conditions at the origin

ϕ⁡(0)=log⁡α,Δ​ϕ​(0)=β0​(α),ϕ′​(0)=(Δ​ϕ)′​(0)=0,\displaystyle\phi(0)=\log\alpha,\quad\Delta\phi(0)=\beta_{0}(\alpha),\quad\phi^{\prime}(0)=(\Delta\phi)^{\prime}(0)=0,

where α>0\alpha>0 and β0(α)∈[−4dα12,0)\beta_{0}(\alpha)\in[-4d\alpha^{\frac{1}{2}},0). Then there exist K0>8​(d−2)K_{0}>8(d-2) and K1>4K_{1}>4 such that

supR>0R4−d​∫0Rrd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r=K0\displaystyle\sup_{R>0}R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr=K_{0} (8.5)

and

supR>0R2−d​∫0Rrd−1​(−Δ)​ϕ​(r)​𝑑r=K1.\displaystyle\sup_{R>0}R^{2-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}(-\Delta)\phi(r)dr=K_{1}. (8.6)
Proof..

As shown in [21, Theorem 1.1], it turns out that when 5≤d≤125\leq d\leq 12, the regular radial solution ϕ\phi of (1.8) subject to the conditions at the origin oscillates around the singular profile −4​log⁡r+log⁡8​(d−4)​(d−2)-4\log r+\log 8(d-4)(d-2), and in particular, the two solutions intersect infinitely many times. Moreover thanks to [21, Theorem 3.1] the regular radial solution ϕ\phi satisfies the following oscillatory asymptotic expansion as r→∞r\to\infty

ϕ⁡(r)=−4​log⁡r+log⁡8​(d−4)​(d−2)+C0​rτ​sin⁡(k0​log​r+k1)+C1​rν+O⁡(r2​τ),\displaystyle\phi(r)=-4\log r+\log 8(d-4)(d-2)+C_{0}r^{\tau}\sin(k_{0}\log r+k_{1})+C_{1}r^{\nu}+O(r^{2\tau}), (8.7)

where τ=−d−42\tau=-\frac{d-4}{2} and ν<2−d\nu<2-d, and for some constants k0,k1,C0,C1k_{0},k_{1},C_{0},C_{1} with C0≠0C_{0}\not=0. Our goal is to show that R4−d​∫0Rrd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r−8​(d−2)R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr-8(d-2) changes sign infinitely many times as R→∞R\to\infty. Using the asymptotic profile (8.7), we write

eϕ⁡(r)=8​(d−4)​(d−2)r4​eε⁡(r)as​r→∞,\displaystyle e^{\phi(r)}=\dfrac{8(d-4)(d-2)}{r^{4}}e^{\varepsilon(r)}\quad\mathrm{as}\ r\to\infty,

where ε⁡(r)=C0​rτ​sin⁡(k0​log⁡r+k1)+C1​rν+O⁡(r2​τ)\varepsilon(r)=C_{0}r^{\tau}\sin(k_{0}\log r+k_{1})+C_{1}r^{\nu}+O(r^{2\tau}). Since ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 as r→∞r\to\infty, we may expand eε⁡(r)e^{\varepsilon(r)} by Taylor’s formula to obtain

eε⁡(r)=1+ε⁡(r)+O⁡(ε​(r)2)as​r→∞.\displaystyle e^{\varepsilon(r)}=1+\varepsilon(r)+O(\varepsilon(r)^{2})\quad\mathrm{as}\ r\to\infty.

Noticing that ε⁡(r)=O⁡(rτ)\varepsilon(r)=O(r^{\tau}) due to (8.7), we deduce

eϕ⁡(r)=8​(d−4)​(d−2)r4​(1+ε⁡(r)+O⁡(r2​τ))as​r→∞.\displaystyle e^{\phi(r)}=\dfrac{8(d-4)(d-2)}{r^{4}}(1+\varepsilon(r)+O(r^{2\tau}))\quad\mathrm{as}\ r\to\infty. (8.8)

Let R0>0R_{0}>0 be sufficiently large so that (8.7) holds for all r≥R0r\geq R_{0}. Then we have

R4−d​∫0Rrd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r=R4−d​∫0R0rd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r+R4−d​∫R0Rrd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r.\displaystyle R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr=R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R_{0}}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr+R^{4-d}\int_{R_{0}}^{R}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr. (8.9)

Since ϕ\phi is regular near the origin, the first term contributes only a bounded quantity. More precisely, there exists a constant K0>0K_{0}>0 such that

R4−d​∫0R0rd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r≤K0​R4−d.\displaystyle R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R_{0}}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr\leq K_{0}R^{4-d}. (8.10)

Therefore, our task is reduced to understanding the asymptotics of the second term in (8.9). Combing (8.8) with the second term on (8.9) yields that for R≥R0R\geq R_{0}

R4−d​∫R0Rrd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r\displaystyle R^{4-d}\int_{R_{0}}^{R}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr =8​(d−4)​(d−2)​R4−d​∫R0Rrd−5​𝑑r\displaystyle=8(d-4)(d-2)R^{4-d}\int_{R_{0}}^{R}r^{d-5}dr
+8(d−4)(d−2)R4−d∫R0Rrd−5ε(r)dr\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt+8(d-4)(d-2)R^{4-d}\int_{R_{0}}^{R}r^{d-5}\varepsilon(r)dr
+8(d−4)(d−2)R4−d∫R0Rrd−5O(r2​τ)dr\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt+8(d-4)(d-2)R^{4-d}\int_{R_{0}}^{R}r^{d-5}O(r^{2\tau})dr
=:I+I​I+I​I​I.\displaystyle=:I+II+III.

The term II can be computed explicitly. Indeed, we have

I=8​(d−2)−8​(d−2)​R0d−4​R4−d,\displaystyle I=8(d-2)-8(d-2)R_{0}^{d-4}R^{4-d}, (8.11)

which implies that I=8​(d−2)+O⁡(R4−d)I=8(d-2)+O(R^{4-d}) as R→∞R\to\infty. With regard to the term I​I​IIII, since d−5+2​τ=−1d-5+2\tau=-1, we can see that there exists C>0C>0 such that

I​I​I≤C​R4−d​log⁡R+C​R4−d​log⁡R0.\displaystyle III\leq CR^{4-d}\log R+CR^{4-d}\log R_{0}. (8.12)

This clearly implies that I​I​I=O⁡(Rτ)III=O(R^{\tau}) as R→∞R\to\infty. As for the term I​III, we expand it as

I​I\displaystyle II =8​(d−4)​(d−2)​C0​R4−d​∫R0Rrd−5+τ​sin⁡(k0​log⁡r+k1)​𝑑r\displaystyle=8(d-4)(d-2)C_{0}R^{4-d}\int_{R_{0}}^{R}r^{d-5+\tau}\sin(k_{0}\log r+k_{1})dr
+8(d−4)(d−2)C1R4−d∫R0Rrd−5+νdr\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt+8(d-4)(d-2)C_{1}R^{4-d}\int_{R_{0}}^{R}r^{d-5+\nu}dr
+8(d−4)(d−2)R4−d∫R0Rrd−5O(r2​τ)dr.\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt+8(d-4)(d-2)R^{4-d}\int_{R_{0}}^{R}r^{d-5}O(r^{2\tau})dr.

Among these contributions, only the first term requires careful attention. Indeed, the remaining two parts are of order O⁡(R4−d)+O⁡(Rν)+O⁡(Rτ)O(R^{4-d})+O(R^{\nu})+O(R^{\tau}), so we may safely disregard them when analyzing the asymptotic behavior. Hereafter, every constant appearing in the computations will be denoted by the same symbol CC. We proceed to observe that

8​(d−4)​(d−2)​C0​R4−d​∫R0Rrd−5+τ​sin⁡(k0​log⁡r+k1)​𝑑r\displaystyle 8(d-4)(d-2)C_{0}R^{4-d}\int_{R_{0}}^{R}r^{d-5+\tau}\sin(k_{0}\log r+k_{1})dr
=C​R4−d​∫R0Rrd−5+τ​sin⁡(k0​log⁡r+k1)​𝑑r\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt=CR^{4-d}\int_{R_{0}}^{R}r^{d-5+\tau}\sin(k_{0}\log r+k_{1})dr
=C​R4−d​∫log⁡R0log⁡Re(d−5+τ)​s​sin⁡(k0​s+k1)​es​𝑑s\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt=CR^{4-d}\int_{\log R_{0}}^{\log R}e^{(d-5+\tau)s}\sin(k_{0}s+k_{1})e^{s}ds
=C​R4−d​∫log⁡R0log⁡Re(d−4+τ)​s​sin⁡(k0​s+k1)​𝑑s.\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt=CR^{4-d}\int_{\log R_{0}}^{\log R}e^{(d-4+\tau)s}\sin(k_{0}s+k_{1})ds. (8.13)

By a standard computation, one can check that

∫log⁡R0log⁡Re(d−4+τ)​s​sin⁡(k0​s+k1)​𝑑s\displaystyle\int_{\log R_{0}}^{\log R}e^{(d-4+\tau)s}\sin(k_{0}s+k_{1})ds =C​Rd−4+τ​sin⁡(k0​log⁡R+k1)\displaystyle=CR^{d-4+\tau}\sin(k_{0}\log R+k_{1})
+C​Rd−4+τ​cos⁡(k0​log⁡R+k1)+C.\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt+CR^{d-4+\tau}\cos(k_{0}\log R+k_{1})+C.

Hence using the trigonometric addition formulas, we obtain

∫log⁡R0log⁡Re(d−4+τ)​s​sin⁡(k0​s+k1)​𝑑s\displaystyle\int_{\log R_{0}}^{\log R}e^{(d-4+\tau)s}\sin(k_{0}s+k_{1})ds =C​Rd−4+τ​sin⁡(k0​log⁡R+θ)+C\displaystyle=CR^{d-4+\tau}\sin(k_{0}\log R+\theta)+C

for some phase shift θ\theta. Combining (8.13) with the identity above yields

C​R4−d​∫R0Rrd−5+τ​sin⁡(k0​log⁡r+k1)​𝑑r=C​Rτ​sin⁡(k0​log⁡R+θ)+C​R4−d.\displaystyle CR^{4-d}\int_{R_{0}}^{R}r^{d-5+\tau}\sin(k_{0}\log r+k_{1})dr=CR^{\tau}\sin(k_{0}\log R+\theta)+CR^{4-d}. (8.14)

Substituting (8.10), (8.11), (8.12), and (8.14) into (8.9), we arrive at

R4−d​∫0Rrd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r−8​(d−2)=C​Rτ​sin⁡(k0​log⁡R+θ)+O⁡(Rτ)as​R→∞\displaystyle R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr-8(d-2)=CR^{\tau}\sin(k_{0}\log R+\theta)+O(R^{\tau})\quad\mathrm{as}\ R\to\infty

for some θ\theta. Since τ<0\tau<0, the above asymptotic expansion immediately implies that

limR→∞R4−d​∫0Rrd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r=8​(d−2).\displaystyle\lim_{R\to\infty}R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr=8(d-2).

Nevertheless, the oscillatory term sin⁡(k0​log⁡R+θ)\sin(k_{0}\log R+\theta) changes sign infinitely many times as R→∞R\to\infty. Thus we obtain the desired conclusion (8.5). Similarly, differentiating the asymptotic expansion of ϕ\phi shows that

−Δ​ϕ​(r)=4​(d−2)​r−2+C0~​rτ−2​sin⁡(k0​log⁡r+θ~)+O⁡(rν−2)+O⁡(r2​τ−2)as​r→∞\displaystyle-\Delta\phi(r)=4(d-2)r^{-2}+\tilde{C_{0}}r^{\tau-2}\sin(k_{0}\log r+\tilde{\theta})+O(r^{\nu-2})+O(r^{2\tau-2})\quad\mathrm{as}\ r\to\infty

for some constant C0~≠0\tilde{C_{0}}\not=0 and some phase shift θ~\tilde{\theta}. Arguing in exactly the same way as above, but now with −Δ​ϕ-\Delta\phi in place of eϕe^{\phi}, we conclude that R2−d​∫0Rrd−1​(−Δ)​ϕ​(r)​𝑑rR^{2-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}(-\Delta)\phi(r)dr oscillates infinitely many times around its limit 44. This completes the proof. ∎

Finally by applying the results of Theorem 1.5, we show that the long-time behavior of the solution to (P) changes dramatically depending on the dimension.

Proof of Theorem 1.8.

(i) Since we have the assumption that the initial data (u0,w0)(u_{0},w_{0}) satisfies

0≤u0≤eϕ,0≤w0≤(−Δ)​ϕfor​all​x∈ℝd,\displaystyle 0\leq u_{0}\leq e^{\phi},\quad 0\leq w_{0}\leq(-\Delta)\phi\quad\mathrm{for\ all}\ x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

according to Theorem 1.5 (i), the solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) of (P) exists globally in time and enjoys the following bounds

∫|x|<Ru⁡(x,t)​𝑑x≤∫|x|<Reϕ⁡(x)​𝑑x,∫|x|<Rw⁡(x,t)​𝑑x≤∫|x|<R(−Δ)​ϕ​(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{|x|<R}u(x,t)dx\leq\int_{|x|<R}e^{\phi(x)}dx,\quad\int_{|x|<R}w(x,t)dx\leq\int_{|x|<R}(-\Delta)\phi(x)dx

for all (R,t)∈(0,∞)×[0,∞)(R,t)\in(0,\infty)\times[0,\infty). From Lemma 8.1, valid for d≥13d\geq 13, we have

supR>0R4−d​∫|x|<Reϕ⁡(x)​𝑑x=8​(d−2)​σd,supR>0R4−d​∫|x|<R(−Δ)​ϕ​(x)​𝑑x=4​σd.\displaystyle\sup_{R>0}R^{4-d}\int_{|x|<R}e^{\phi(x)}dx=8(d-2)\sigma_{d},\quad\sup_{R>0}R^{4-d}\int_{|x|<R}(-\Delta)\phi(x)dx=4\sigma_{d}.

Thus the upper bounds claimed in (1.15) follow.

(ii) If 5≤d≤125\leq d\leq 12, then, in light of Lemma 8.2, we can choose a parameter λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1) so that λ​K0≤8​(d−2)\lambda K_{0}\leq 8(d-2) and λ​K1≤4\lambda K_{1}\leq 4, where the constants K0K_{0} and K1K_{1} are those provided in Lemma 8.2. Therefore whenever the initial data (u0,w0)(u_{0},w_{0}) satisfy

0≤u0≤λ​eϕ,0≤w0≤λ⁡(−Δ)​ϕfor​all​x∈ℝd,\displaystyle 0\leq u_{0}\leq\lambda e^{\phi},\quad 0\leq w_{0}\leq\lambda(-\Delta)\phi\quad\mathrm{for\ all}\ x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

from Theorem 1.5, we conclude that the solution exists globally in time and satisfy the estimates (1.15). ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.10.

(i) Let λ>1\lambda>1. Assume that the initial data (u0,w0)(u_{0},w_{0}) are given by (u0,w0)=(λ​eϕ,λ⁡(−Δ)​ϕ)(u_{0},w_{0})=(\lambda e^{\phi},\lambda(-\Delta)\phi), where ϕ∈C4​(ℝd)\phi\in C^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is a radially symmetric solution of (1.8) with the initial conditions:

ϕ⁡(0)=log⁡α,Δ​ϕ​(0)=β0​(α),ϕ′​(0)=(Δ​ϕ)′​(0)=0,\displaystyle\phi(0)=\log\alpha,\quad\Delta\phi(0)=\beta_{0}(\alpha),\quad\phi^{\prime}(0)=(\Delta\phi)^{\prime}(0)=0,

where α>0\alpha>0 and β0(α)∈[−4dα12,0)\beta_{0}(\alpha)\in[-4d\alpha^{\frac{1}{2}},0). According to Theorem 1.5, the corresponding solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) obtained via Proposition 3.8 blows up in finite time. Moreover, Lemma 8.1 yields that

supR>0R4−d​∫0Rrd−1​u0​(r)​𝑑r\displaystyle\sup_{R>0}R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}u_{0}(r)dr =λ​supR>0R4−d​∫0Rrd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r\displaystyle=\lambda\sup_{R>0}R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr
=8​(d−2)​λ\displaystyle=8(d-2)\lambda
>8​(d−2)\displaystyle>8(d-2)

and similarly,

supR>0R2−d​∫0Rrd−1​w0​(r)​𝑑r=4​λ>4.\displaystyle\sup_{R>0}R^{2-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}w_{0}(r)dr=4\lambda>4.

This completes the proof.

(ii) Let λ∈(0,1]\lambda\in(0,1] so that

λ​K0>8​(d−2),λ​K1>4,\displaystyle\lambda K_{0}>8(d-2),\quad\lambda K_{1}>4,

where K0K_{0} and K1K_{1} are the constants in Lemma 8.2. In analogy with (i), the initial data are chosen to be (u0,w0)=(λ​eϕ,λ⁡(−Δ)​ϕ)(u_{0},w_{0})=(\lambda e^{\phi},\lambda(-\Delta)\phi), where the same function ϕ\phi is employed. In light of Theorem 1.5, the solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) established by Proposition 3.8 exists globally in time, nevertheless Lemma 8.2 implies that the initial data (u0,w0)(u_{0},w_{0}) satisfies the following condition

supR>0R4−d​∫0Rrd−1​u0​(r)​𝑑r\displaystyle\sup_{R>0}R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}u_{0}(r)dr =λ​supR>0R4−d​∫0Rrd−1​eϕ⁡(r)​𝑑r=λ​K0>8​(d−2)\displaystyle=\lambda\sup_{R>0}R^{4-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}e^{\phi(r)}dr=\lambda K_{0}>8(d-2)

and moreover

supR>0R2−d​∫0Rrd−1​w0​(r)​𝑑r=λ​K1>4.\displaystyle\sup_{R>0}R^{2-d}\int_{0}^{R}r^{d-1}w_{0}(r)dr=\lambda K_{1}>4.

Thus we arrive at the desired conclusion. ∎
